Ask, Don’t Equip: Question-Driven Coding Agents
for Deep Kernel Optimization

 

Gabriele Oliaro 1 2  Jaeseong Lee 1  Zhaoyuan Su 1  Sreeram Vennam 2  Zhihao Jia 2  Samyam Rajbhandari 1 

††footnotetext: 1Snowflake AI Research 2Carnegie Mellon University. Correspondence to: Gabriele Oliaro <goliaro@cs.cmu.edu>.
Preprint.
Abstract

LLM agents for GPU kernel optimization sit at two ends of a structure–freedom tradeoff. Scripted agents fix what the model does at each step, via a learned policy, an optimization menu, or fixed roles, and are sample-efficient where the recipe applies and stall where it does not. Open-ended agents let a self-directed model mutate a population of kernels and pay for the freedom in trials: thousands of evaluations, repeated edits, and wrong candidates. Both respond to hard targets by equipping the agent with more: parsed profiler output, disassembly analysis, retrieval over documentation and libraries, and stores of lessons. We argue that both lack direction, a hypothesis about where the remaining gap is, and that a short question asked at the right moment supplies it without narrowing what the agent may do next. We present KernelSeek, a question-driven agent that makes an existing CUDA kernel faster with no operator-specific knowledge and no faster implementation to imitate: a general-purpose coding agent, a minimal harness that enforces a verifiable goal, and questions at decision points, first from a human, then from a bank the agent applies to itself. On the same task, evaluator, hardware, and week, a tool-rich autonomous agent built in the prevailing style plateaued at 0.50×\times FlashAttention-3 after 133 model-driven steps; KernelSeek reached 1.13×\times. It then produced dependency-free FlashAttention forward kernels for Hopper and Blackwell, single CUDA files with no CUTLASS, CuTe, cuBLAS, or cuDNN, correct on all 182 scenarios per architecture and 1.16×\times FlashAttention-3 and 1.46×\times FlashAttention-4 (geometric mean). Across 162 human messages and 11.5K agent tool calls, every large gain followed a question that moved the agent to a different layer of the system or rejected a claimed limit, never one that supplied information. We release the kernels, harness, question bank, and all traces.

1 Introduction

GPU kernels are one of the main levers on the efficiency of large language model training and serving Miao et al. (2025). Attention is the clearest case: each GPU generation has required a new implementation to reach the hardware’s potential, from FlashAttention on Ampere Dao et al. (2022); Dao (2024) to FlashAttention-3 on Hopper Shah et al. (2024) and FlashAttention-4 on Blackwell Zadouri and others (2026), each rewrite reporting a 1.5–2×\times speedup over its predecessor Dao (2024); Shah et al. (2024), and serving systems ship specialized attention engines of their own Kwon et al. (2023); Ye et al. (2025); Miao et al. (2024). Such kernels are deep targets: their performance hinges on whole-pipeline choreography (warp-specialized producers and consumers, asynchronous tensor-core MMAs, copies ordered by barrier phases, register budgets, persistent schedulers, the host dispatch path) rather than on local edits, their correctness hinges on hardware invariants that documentation states only in passing, and they must win across a production feature surface of paged caches, grouped heads, masks, ragged batches, split decode, and low precision rather than on one shape. Domain-specific languages Tillet et al. (2019); Spector et al. (2025) and template libraries Thakkar et al. (2023) lower the barrier, but state-of-the-art kernels still take expert teams months per architecture Shah et al. (2024); Zadouri and others (2026), and NVIDIA’s own production kernels sit well below the hardware’s speed of light on many shapes Lin and others (2026).

Kernel generation has therefore become an active application of LLM coding agents, with benchmarks Ouyang et al. (2025); Xing et al. (2026); Lin and others (2026); Oliaro et al. (2026), models trained with reinforcement learning to emit kernels Baronio et al. (2026); Li et al. (2026); Dai et al. (2026); Liu et al. (2026), agentic pipelines Hong et al. (2025); Wei et al. (2025); Sun et al. (2026b), evolutionary search with an LLM as the mutation operator Novikov et al. (2025); Lange et al. (2025a); Chen et al. (2026), and deployments across whole production backends Liao and others (2025); Cursor and NVIDIA (2026). These agents sit at the two ends of a structure–freedom tradeoff. Scripted agents fix in advance what the model does at each step: a generate–test–refine loop with a learned policy Baronio et al. (2026); Li et al. (2026); Liu et al. (2026), a menu of optimizations Hong et al. (2025), a team with fixed roles Wei et al. (2025); Sun et al. (2026b), or a harness in which humans gate every promotion Shui et al. (2026). The script makes them sample-efficient but encodes what to try: Autocomp’s performance collapses without its optimization menu Hong et al. (2025), and fixed-loop RL that is competitive on single operators fails on fused models Liu et al. (2026); Zhu et al. (2026); Dai et al. (2026). Open-ended agents let an LLM mutate a population of programs Romera-Paredes et al. (2024); Novikov et al. (2025); Lange et al. (2025a); Guo et al. (2025); Wiedemann et al. (2026), and AVO makes a self-directed coding agent the variation operator itself Chen et al. (2026). The freedom buys results, up to 10.5% over FA4 for AVO Chen et al. (2026) and a 32% speedup of a FlashAttention kernel for AlphaEvolve Novikov et al. (2025), and is paid for in trials: AVO’s agent explored more than 500 directions over seven days to commit 40 versions and needed a supervisor to break cycles of failing edits Chen et al. (2026), about 30% of the lines such agents add are byte-identical to lines they deleted earlier Pelleriti et al. (2026), and 30–55% of LLM-evolved CUDA candidates are incorrect Guo et al. (2025); Varadharajan et al. (2026).

We argue that what both ends lack is direction: a hypothesis about where the remaining gap is. A script hard-codes direction and cannot supply it where the script is wrong; open-ended search samples for it, and samples poorly, because LLMs are not open-ended optimizers. They search greedily from their priors Redko et al. (2026), anchor on the solution in the prompt Jones and Steinhardt (2022), stop early out of conservatism or after a run of failures Merouani et al. (2025), cycle through near-duplicate variants Li et al. (2025); Dong et al. (2025), and report completion the environment contradicts Advani (2026). Information is not what is missing: both ends already hand the agent profilers, documentation, and reference implementations Chen et al. (2026); MIT HAN Lab (2026), and such feedback helps only when it supplies the specific thing the model lacks, which profiler and compiler output rarely does Redko et al. (2026). What moves the same models is a hypothesis posed from outside: intrinsic self-correction fails where external feedback succeeds Huang et al. (2024), a human’s feedback on a model’s own code raised repair success by 1.57×\times through structural changes the model did not propose Olausson et al. (2024), and in the FlashInfer kernel contest, agents given expert directions beat the same agents running alone on every kernel Shui et al. (2026). Our reading, and our traces, say that a question changes the task. “Make this faster” is open-ended, and the model answers it greedily. “Is the baseline winning on kernel cycles or only on wall-clock?” is bounded, and to answer it the model will tear out and rewrite a part of the kernel it would never touch on its own. A well-placed question supplies direction without narrowing what the agent may do next, which neither more structure, more freedom, nor more tooling can.

This paper presents KernelSeek, a question-driven agent for optimizing CUDA kernels. KernelSeek takes an existing kernel as its seed and makes it faster; it is not tied to an operator, and it does not need a faster implementation to imitate. It keeps the freedom of the open-ended agents, a general-purpose coding agent with no script and no pre-digested context, and recovers the efficiency of the scripted ones by supplying direction at decision points: when progress stalls, when the agent claims a limit or completion, and after suspiciously large wins. Its only purpose-built component is a minimal harness that checks every candidate against the seed’s outputs and an fp32 reference, times every scenario against the seed, and states the goal as a stop condition that is verified rather than requested. A good question contains no answer: it names a hypothesis the agent has not considered, and testing it takes a measurement the agent can make with ordinary tools. Questions that recur harden into a bank the agent applies to itself, and KernelSeek composes with evolutionary search by wrapping the same agent in an AVO-style lineage whose directives are questions.

We evaluate KernelSeek on a case study chosen because a strong upstream exists to measure against: FA3- and FA4-class attention kernels as single CUDA files with no CUTLASS, CuTe, cuBLAS, or cuDNN, across the feature surface that vLLM exposes, with the upstream kernels as correctness oracle and yardstick. Against an autonomous agent we built for the same task in the style of AVO and its successors, with an orchestrated loop, pre-digested profiles, documentation retrieval, and a store of learned lessons, KernelSeek reached 1.13×\times FA3 in geometric mean over the same 26 configurations on the same machine in the same week, where the autonomous agent plateaued at 0.50×\times after 133 model-driven steps (Figure 1). Carried through to full campaigns, KernelSeek produced fa3_hopper.cu and fa4_blackwell.cu, correct on all 182 Hopper and all runnable Blackwell scenarios, at 1.16×\times FA3 and 1.46×\times FA4 in geomean, including 1.10×\times FA4 on production shapes from SOL-ExecBench Lin and others (2026). Across the 16 sessions that produced them, KernelSeek made 11.5K tool calls per 162 human messages: asking did not mean using fewer tools, but using them on the right thing.

This paper makes three contributions.

  • •

    We identify the failure modes of autonomous agents on deep kernel targets that neither more structure, more freedom, nor more tooling fixes, and show them co-occurring in a tool-rich agent built to the prevailing recipe (§3).

  • •

    We present KernelSeek, an operator-agnostic question-driven kernel agent built from a minimal harness, a verifiable goal, and a reusable question bank, and show how it composes with evolutionary search (§2).

  • •

    We compare KernelSeek with the equipped agent on the same task, evaluator, hardware, and week, analyze 162 human messages and 11.5K tool calls to show which questions redirected the agent and why (§5), and release fa3_hopper.cu and fa4_blackwell.cu, to our knowledge the fastest open-source FA3- and FA4-class forward kernels on the scenarios we evaluate, with the harness, question bank, and complete traces of both approaches (§4).

2 KernelSeek: A Question-Driven Kernel Agent

KernelSeek takes a working CUDA kernel, a set of scenarios, and a goal, and returns a faster kernel whose outputs match the seed on every scenario. It has three parts: a minimal harness that makes the goal verifiable, a general-purpose coding agent with no script around it, and a source of questions at the moments the agent is about to go wrong. The questions come from a human steerer or, once they recur, from a bank the agent applies to itself. Nothing in the method is specific to an operator, and nothing requires a faster implementation to exist.

2.1 Ask vs. Equip: A Common Frame

Kernel optimization by an agent is a search. A candidate is a kernel source; its fitness is a vector of per-scenario speedups over the seed, collapsed to zero if any scenario is incorrect; and the lineage is monotone, as in AVO Chen et al. (2026). The agent is the variation operator: it proposes the next candidate conditioned on a context, and everything a designer can do is a choice of what enters that context and when. An equipped agent receives the task, tools whose output has been distilled for it (a profiler parser that names the bottleneck, a disassembly differ), knowledge retrieved for it (documentation sections, hints mined from reference libraries, a store of lessons), the lineage, and feedback on the last candidate; the designer improves it by adding tools and knowledge. Our baseline (§3) is a serious instance. An asked agent receives the task, the harness’s output, the lineage, and, at decision points, a short question. It still has every tool a developer machine offers, the compiler, profiler, disassembler, sanitizer, and debugger, but nothing is pre-digested, and direction arrives as a question rather than a menu. The designer improves it by asking better questions.

2.2 A Minimal Harness and a Verifiable Goal

The only component we build is the evaluator. One command builds a candidate, checks its outputs against the seed’s and an fp32 reference on every scenario, and times it against the seed back to back on the same GPU, reporting per-scenario ratios and their geometric mean. Other kernels the user cares about can be added as measured comparison columns, but none is required. Constraints are stated once and enforced mechanically: in the case study, the ban on CUTLASS, CuTe, cuBLAS, and cuDNN is checked by inspecting the built binary’s symbols.

The goal is a predicate over the evaluator’s output, enforced rather than requested. We install it as a Stop hook in the coding agent: whenever the agent attempts to end its turn, the hook evaluates the predicate and, if any clause is unmet, returns the agent to work with the unmet clauses in hand. A predicate such as “at least parity with the seed on every scenario” removes the most common failure of autonomous agents, declaring completion early. Two lessons shaped how we write predicates. They must quantify over every scenario rather than an aggregate, because an agent will otherwise satisfy the aggregate on the shapes it is good at. And they must not be judged by a model where they can be computed: the one time our hook delegated the verdict to a model judge, it accepted a premature claim that a human then overturned (§5.4).

2.3 Questions: What They Are and When to Ask

Across the traces, the questions that preceded the largest gains share six properties. They carry no answer: they name a class of hypothesis and leave the derivation to the agent. They demand a measurement the agent can make with the tools it has, so the answer is a number rather than an opinion. They move across layers of the system, from the kernel to the host launch path to the routing logic to the benchmark itself, where an agent left alone stays at the layer it started at. They refuse premature closure by asking whether a claimed limit is a property of the hardware or of the agent’s own design. They are cheap, tens of tokens against the tens of thousands that retrieved documentation costs Liu et al. (2024); LangChain (2025). And they counteract deference: an agent tends to keep the structure it started from and accept the framing it is given Sharma et al. (2024), and a question asks it to justify that choice with evidence.

Eight categories cover the questions a human asked during the case study (Table 4 in Appendix A): measurement check (13 messages), bound differencing (10), benchmark validity (7), gap triage (7), agent process (6), challenge a limit (5), strategy options (5), and hypothesis check (3). The largest checks a measurement: whether a win is noise, whether a comparison is fair, whether the agent is timing what it thinks it is timing. The second pits the agent’s claimed ceiling against an independent estimate of what is achievable. In the case study that estimate was often the upstream kernel, but the pattern does not depend on one existing: a roofline, a speed-of-light figure Lin and others (2026), or an A/B that swaps only the launcher around an identical binary serves the same role. Questions are asked at decision points, not continuously; the traces show five: at the start of a campaign, to fix the scope; at a plateau; when the agent claims a limit or completion; after a suspiciously large win; and when correctness breaks in a way the agent explains away. Between these points the agent works alone, about 71 tool calls per human message, where the median message is a sentence or two. The steerer contributes no code and no CUDA knowledge the agent lacks; it contributes doubt, at the right moment, about the right thing.

2.4 The Question Bank

After the campaigns we distilled the recurring questions into a bank. Its first version, taken from the traces alone, had 48 entries, and reading it back showed the hazard of distilling from one case study: 21 named the upstream kernel as the comparison and 13 named attention structure. The released bank removes both. A question is admitted only if it carries no answer, is answerable by a measurement with stock tools, is phrased against a bound (a roofline or a per-tile cycle budget) rather than a reference, names an architecture only as a parameter, and names no operator. To cover the aspects a single attention campaign never exercised, we also mined three public GEMM worklogs on Ampere, Hopper, and Blackwell Boehm (2022); Shankhdhar (2024); Modular Inc. (2025) and the FlashAttention-3 and -4 papers Shah et al. (2024); Zadouri and others (2026) for the diagnostic that preceded each of their optimizations, and phrased it as a question. The result has 101 core entries in ten groups ordered by where the gap might be (scope and triage; the bound and the regime; harness and measurement; host, launch, and routing; memory hierarchy; compute issue; occupancy and registers; asynchrony and pipelining; scheduling; low-precision numerics), five that apply only when another implementation is available to measure, and eighteen per-architecture checklist entries that bind the generic mechanisms to Ampere, Hopper, or Blackwell instructions. Operator structure enters through a plug-in with five slots (regimes, irregular work, non-MMA units, reduction splits, indirect loads); the attention plug-in fills them with prefill and decode, causal masks, softmax, split-KV, and paged gathers. Appendix A lists the bank with provenance tags: 29 entries carry a trace tag, and the 72 from public sources alone are untested.

2.5 From Asking the Agent to the Agent Asking Itself

Because the questions recur, they can be handed to the agent as part of its instructions. We codify them as a skill with five parts: the goal, the hard rules the harness enforces, a loop, a list of questions to ask itself, and the commands that run the evaluator and profiler. The loop is the bank in procedural form: fix the scope; measure the seed; classify each gap as host, routing, or kernel before touching code; bound it; form a hypothesis; rewrite; gate. At each step the agent fans out subagents, one per hypothesis, each returning a hypothesis and the measurement that tests it rather than a patch. The skill is parameterized by the seed, the scenario set, and the goal; its questions were reused across the Hopper and Blackwell campaigns nearly verbatim.

2.6 Composing with Evolutionary Search

KernelSeek is compatible with the evolutionary loops of the open-ended agents, because it changes the variation operator’s direction rather than the loop around it. We wrap the same agent in an AVO-style search Chen et al. (2026): a monotone lineage, several diverse mutations per generation applied to isolated copies and scored by the evaluator, and a strategist that reviews the trajectory and writes the next generation’s directives. The one change is that the directives are questions, hypotheses to test rather than edits to make. As §5.5 shows, evolution amplifies direction; it does not supply it.

2.7 Hypotheses

The evaluation tests five claims. H1 (quality): on the same task, evaluator, and hardware, the asked agent reaches higher performance at full correctness than the equipped one. H2 (efficiency): with fewer model-driven steps and GPU-hours, counting human time. H3 (mechanism): the largest gains follow questions that change the layer under consideration or reject a claimed limit, not questions that supply information. H4 (complementarity): evolutionary search amplifies the effect of questions and does not substitute for them. H5 (generality): the questions that moved the case study contain nothing specific to the operator or to a reference once the reference is replaced by a bound.

3 Baseline: A Tool-Rich Autonomous Evolutionary Agent

Before KernelSeek, we built the agent the prevailing recipe prescribes. Arsenal is an autonomous evolutionary agent for the Hopper half of the case study (§4), in the lineage of AVO, KDA, and CUCo Chen et al. (2026); MIT HAN Lab (2026); Varadharajan et al. (2026): an orchestrated loop, a profiler whose output is distilled for the model, retrieval over documentation and reference libraries, a typed knowledge store, and no human in the loop by design. Its failure is the paper’s motivation, and its evaluator, unchanged, scored the first KernelSeek session in the head-to-head of §5.3.

Design.

The task was a single dependency-free CUDA file implementing vLLM’s FA3 operator for H200, with success defined as at least parity with FA3 on 26 configurations and token-for-token equality with FA3 on a greedy decode in vLLM. A deterministic Python orchestrator owns the loop. Each step generates one candidate, builds it, checks for forbidden dependencies by inspecting the binary’s symbols, analyzes the SASS instruction mix, verifies correctness on all 26 configurations, times it against FA3 interleaved across four GPUs, profiles the worst configuration with NCU, and, on promotion, A/B-tests it inside a live vLLM instance. It then writes a lesson to a memory file, a note to the knowledge store, and an entry to a lever ledger, checks for a plateau, and checkpoints. A Claude Opus model (claude-opus-4-8) running headless in Claude Code is the brain, invoked in a fresh session at every step. The orchestrator decides what to try and the brain decides how: sixteen hand-written levers, from tensor-core MMAs and TMA loads to warp specialization and persistent scheduling, are keyed to the bottleneck label the NCU parser assigns, and the chosen lever is placed in the prompt with the instruction to write the improved candidate. Everything else the brain sees is distilled by a component (Appendix E): a bottleneck diagnosis, retrieved documentation, hints extracted from DeepGEMM, ThunderKittens, and CUTLASS, and typed knowledge-store notes. The median step prompt was 22.6K characters, 37% of it pre-fetched reference material, plus the current best kernel re-read each step. Promotion is greedy on the worst-case configuration ratio with a 3% noise band, and a plateau detector opens rewrite branches. No human-authored text ever entered a step prompt.

Outcome.

The run kept 313 steps over 4.2 days, with a further 117 discarded by three human rollbacks. The model was active for steps 0 to 132, about 62 hours and $660 of API usage over 253 sessions; from step 133 the brain’s credentials had expired and the loop re-scored old kernels until stopped, so we report 133 model-driven steps as the budget. The best candidate reached 0.50×\times FA3 in geometric mean with a worst case of 0.24×\times; no configuration reached parity. All progress happened by step 35, in about 45 hours. The remaining 98 model-driven steps produced nothing beyond noise: the final champion, from step 112, is byte-identical to the candidate of step 104 and was promoted because one of 54 re-measurements of the same source landed above the noise band. Correctness was not the problem: 312 of 313 candidates were correct.

Why it stalled.

The traces show the failure modes of §1, each with a number attached. Information was not the constraint: with more than a third of every prompt devoted to reference material and 1.6 GB of reference code on disk, 82% of the characters the brain read through its own tool calls were its own kernel, and its 92 documentation lookups over 246 sessions mostly justified not making a change. The menu bounded the search: 36 of the 37 rewrite branches the plateau detector opened were seeded from the same step, and every candidate after step 35 was a local edit of the same design. Memory hardened conclusions, not evidence: the memory file recorded one configuration as “DEFINITIVE[ly] …walled by [the] 65536-reg file”, a wall FA3 does not hit, and the brain’s summary at step 112 was that “the only remaining escape is a clean-sheet 1-blk/SM warp-spec persistent seed, which is outside this branch’s mandate and measured to lose”; each fresh session inherited earlier verdicts without the reasoning behind them, and nothing in the loop was positioned to doubt them. Every diagnostic lived at one layer: NCU, the SASS analyzer, and the sanitizer all examine the kernel, while the gap KernelSeek later closed on this evaluator was in the host launch path (§5.4). The objective rewarded caution: promoting on the worst configuration inside a noise band accepted noise as progress and could not fund a restructuring that regresses before it pays off; 312 correct candidates out of 313 is the signature of a search that never took a risk.

Three lessons carried into KernelSeek: the mechanical parts of the harness were worth keeping, and KernelSeek’s harness is this evaluator with the orchestration removed; everything built to inform the brain could go, and the knowledge store was actively harmful; and the loop lacked one input, a reason to doubt a conclusion and a hypothesis about where else to look.

4 Case Study: Dependency-Free FlashAttention for Hopper and Blackwell

Task.

We asked KernelSeek to produce a FlashAttention forward kernel for Hopper and one for Blackwell, each a single CUDA file with no CUTLASS, CuTe, cuBLAS, or cuDNN, exposing the operator schema vLLM uses for FlashAttention-3 so that the result drops in for the upstream kernel and is timed against it from identical inputs. The scenario suites mirror the upstream kernels’ own test grids and add production shapes from SOL-ExecBench Lin and others (2026): 182 scenarios per architecture spanning bf16, fp16, and fp8; paged and contiguous KV caches; MHA, GQA, and MQA; causal, sliding-window, softcapped, and attention-sink masking; ragged batches; prefill, chunked prefill, and split-KV decode; and unequal query and value head dimensions. The breadth is deliberate, since kernels scored on a few shapes report speedups that shrink on the production path Oliaro et al. (2026). The goal was correctness on every scenario and at least parity with upstream in geometric mean. The seed in both cases was a slow but general kernel (a scalar one-warp-per-query kernel on Hopper, a one-warpgroup dense-only skeleton on Blackwell), and anything the fast paths did not yet cover fell back to it, so correctness held throughout. The upstream kernels, FA3 as shipped in vLLM and the CuteDSL FA4 Shah et al. (2024); Zadouri and others (2026), were the correctness oracle and the yardstick the goal was stated against. The dependency-free constraint means the layouts, descriptors, pipelines, and register allocation that CUTLASS and CuteDSL derive for the upstream kernels had to be written by hand Thakkar et al. (2023).

What the agent built.

On Hopper, fa3_hopper.cu (3.6K lines) is a warp-specialized kernel in raw CUDA and PTX: producer and consumer warpgroups connected by a TMA and mbarrier ring, asynchronous wgmma MMAs with setmaxnreg register rebalancing, persistent scheduling with inter-warpgroup ping-pong, split-KV decode with a combine pass, and a native fp8 path. Its one remaining limit sits where a library’s allocator would otherwise be: at head dimension 256 the hand-written swizzle composes only at a few tile widths and the output accumulator caps occupancy at one CTA per SM, so that scenario runs at 0.94×\times. On Blackwell, fa4_blackwell.cu (10.2K lines) is a family with host-side routing, a structure the questions pushed the agent toward after a single kernel had stalled (§5.4): a persistent warp-specialized collective for the dense envelope (two stacked 128-row query halves, two softmax warpgroups in an ordered ping-pong, a correction warpgroup rescaling the output in tensor memory, one MMA warp driving tcgen05), variants for unequal head dimensions and paged prefill, and a two-tile kernel for small, ragged, and decode shapes. Several decisive gains were outside the kernel bodies: a synchronous host copy costing about 38 μ\mus per call, a stale routing gate, a TMA gather issued from divergent lanes, and ring state the compiler had placed in local memory. fp8 inputs and dense head dimensions of 192 and above are not yet built on Blackwell (28 of 182 scenarios).

Results.

Table 1 summarizes the outcome; Appendix B plots every scenario. Both kernels are correct on every scenario they run, and both beat upstream in geometric mean. fa3_hopper.cu runs at 1.16×\times FA3 with 135 of 182 scenarios at or above parity; the wins are concentrated in ragged prefill, paged and speculative decode, and the masking grid, while the paper-style sweeps of the claim set are at parity and dense fp8 prefill is the one clear hole at 0.67×\times. fa4_blackwell.cu runs at 1.46×\times FA4 across the 124 scenarios FA4 also runs, with 98 at or above parity and a worst case of 0.78×\times. The headline shrinks as the baseline strengthens: cuDNN is the fastest baseline on 54 of 182 Hopper scenarios and on 92 of 124 Blackwell ones, where it wins dense prefill and batched decode outright, so the kernels are 1.10×\times and 1.07×\times the fastest available implementation, and at or above it on production shapes. Three caveats are documented in Appendix B: the edge sets consist of short kernels, so part of their 1.5–2×\times is upstream dispatch overhead; the largest claim wins are fp8-KV decode shapes on which FA4 is slow, and excluding them moves the Blackwell all-set geomeans to 1.37, 1.32, and 1.08×\times; and one paged-KV fast path depends on physically consecutive pages. Every Blackwell scenario below parity has a measured cause: dense long context spends identical tensor work over a third more cycles because of twice as many barrier waits per block, batched decode pays a cold start per CTA, and head dimension 96 runs on a padded 128-wide path. On Hopper the losses are fp8 dense prefill, softcapped prefill, head dimension 96, and long sliding windows (0.34–0.79×\times); these have not been profiled to the same depth.

Release.

We release both kernels under Apache 2.0 with the evaluator, the PTX probes used to validate each Blackwell primitive in isolation, the search scripts (§2.6), the question bank and skill, and the complete agent traces of both approaches. The kernels are meant as seeds, with their residual gaps measured, so that the next agent starts from a known frontier.

5 Evaluation

We ask five questions, one per hypothesis of §2.7. RQ1: how fast and how correct are the kernels? RQ2: on the same task, evaluator, hardware, and week, how does KernelSeek compare with the equipped agent? RQ3: which human messages redirected the agent, and how? RQ4: what does evolutionary search add on top of questions? RQ5: do the questions transfer?

5.1 Setup

Hopper experiments and the head-to-head ran on one 8×\timesH200 node; Blackwell experiments on one 8×\timesB200 node. The upstream kernels are vLLM’s FA3 and the CuteDSL FA4 at pinned commits; cuDNN’s fused attention (9.20 on Hopper, 9.19 on Blackwell) and FlashInfer are comparison columns fed the same buffers. Implementations are timed back to back on one idle GPU with an L2 flush before each sample; clocks are not locked, so only ratios are reported; four independent Hopper batches agree to within 0.3% on every aggregate (Appendix F). The equipped agent ran claude-opus-4-8 through Claude Code in headless mode, one fresh session per step. KernelSeek sessions used two front-ends: Claude Code with the Stop-hook goal, on claude-opus-4-8 for seven sessions and claude-opus-5 for the last two, and Cursor with the same instructions and without the hook, whose exports do not record the model. Sixteen KernelSeek sessions are archived, nine in Claude Code and seven in Cursor, from June 17 to August 7, 2026: twelve for the Hopper campaign and four for Blackwell. They contain 162 human messages and 11,532 agent tool calls, 8,791 in the parent sessions and 2,741 in subagents. One author labeled each human message by its primary act (goal, directive, question, approval, correction), flagged interrogative phrasing, and assigned questions to the eight categories of §2.3; tool calls were classified by target (Appendix D).

5.2 RQ1: Kernel Performance

The kernels are reported in §4. In brief: fa3_hopper.cu is correct on all 182 Hopper scenarios at 1.16×\times FA3 and 1.10×\times the fastest available implementation including cuDNN; fa4_blackwell.cu is correct on all 154 runnable Blackwell scenarios at 1.46×\times FA4 and 1.07×\times the fastest available. Per-scenario Hopper ratios vary by 1% at the median and 6% at most across repeats. Every Blackwell scenario below parity has a measured root cause (Appendix B). This is H1’s quality half, and the result the rest of the section explains.

5.3 RQ2: Head-to-Head on the Same Task

The comparison is controlled in the ways that matter. During its first Hopper session, KernelSeek adopted the equipped agent’s own evaluator, the same 26 configurations, FA3 baseline, and correctness gate, on the same machine, in overlapping days. Table 2 and Figure 1 give the outcome. The equipped agent’s lineage champion reached 0.48×\times FA3 at step 35, after 44.7 hours, and did not improve in the remaining 98 model-driven steps (§3). Its worst configuration stayed at 0.24×\times and none reached parity. KernelSeek started from 0.009×\times, because its kernel of the time routed the evaluator’s paged and grouped-query configurations to the scalar fallback, and reached 0.96×\times after 21 hours, 1.02×\times after 66, and 1.13×\times after 68, of which 26.7 were an idle gap. At the end, 22 of 26 configurations were at or above parity and the worst was 0.87×\times. This supports H1 and, counting the 40 human turns against 133 steps and 62 model-hours, H2.

Three caveats qualify the comparison: KernelSeek had built a kernel for FA3’s 40-scenario test grid in the two preceding days, so the 0.009×\times start understates its head start; the front-ends differ, and token usage is not recoverable for the Cursor sessions; and each arm is a single run. The fair reading is that in one calendar week a steered agent crossed parity on an evaluator on which an unsteered one, given more compute, did not reach half of it. We treat Table 2 as showing that the gap exists and is large, and RQ3 as the evidence for why.

Where the effort went.

The lower block of Table 2 contrasts tool use. The equipped agent received a third of its context as pre-fetched reference material, yet spent 82% of what it read on its own kernel. KernelSeek, with nothing pushed to it, spent 26% on its own kernels and ran the profiler 429 times on raw output. The questions did not reduce tool use; they aimed it.

5.4 RQ3: Anatomy of the Questions

What the human said.

Of the 162 human messages, directives are the largest class (58, 36%), followed by questions (44, 27%), approvals (30, 19%), corrections (19, 12%), and goals (11, 7%); 63 messages (39%) are interrogative in phrasing, and 12 of the 19 corrections are phrased as questions (Appendix D). The steering was interrogative, not mostly questions: directives and approvals keep the agent moving, and the questions are where its course changed. The agent also asked. Across the Claude Code sessions it posed 35 structured questions to the human, 24 of which offered an option to accept the current state or stop, and its messages assert a limit or an impossibility 126 times. The Stop hook returned it to work 59 times. Autonomous agents seek closure; the harness and the human refused it.

Which questions mattered.

Table 3 walks through six turning points we can verify in the archived traces. Two patterns stand out. First, every large jump followed a question that either moved the agent to a different layer (from kernel tuning to the per-configuration table, to the host launch path, to the benchmark itself) or rejected a claimed limit; none followed a message that supplied information the agent lacked, which supports H3. Second, the measurement the question triggered was always one the agent could already make: the per-configuration table, the host-side profile, the sanitizer, and the debugger were available at every earlier step. What the agent lacked was a reason to look. Four further episodes, among them the 38 μ\mus host copy and a routing sweep that moved the Blackwell geomean from 0.88 to 1.15×\times without changing a kernel body, are documented in the repository’s history but not in archived sessions, and we cite them as outcomes only.

5.5 RQ4: Questions and Evolutionary Search

We wrapped the same agent in the loop of §2.6 and ran it on the Blackwell dense-prefill kernel from a correct but slow port (Figure 3, Appendix D). The first generation, whose directive asked whether a persistent schedule with longest-first ordering and cross-tile overlap would recover the lost overlap, took the kernel from 0.29×\times to 0.68×\times. Three more generations added 0.10×\times between them through a folded softmax scale, a split K/V barrier, and a depth-two softmax–correction handshake, while directives on register rebalancing and address hoisting measured neutral or negative. The search stalled at 0.78×\times with the kernel’s own cycle count already below upstream’s. The last 22 points came from a question, not a generation: asked where the time was going, the agent profiled the whole call rather than the kernel and found that synchronous host copies accounted for the gap. Evolution amplified the direction the directives carried and searched efficiently within the layer it was pointed at; it could not move to a layer it was not pointed at. This is H4.

5.6 RQ5: Reuse

The question categories were populated mostly during the Hopper campaign, which came first. Five of the eight recur in the Blackwell campaign, and the Blackwell skill’s self-questions restate Hopper questions nearly verbatim. Of the 63 interrogative messages, 17 mention a concept specific to attention and 32 mention the upstream kernel; the rest name only measurements, layers, and process, and where a question names the upstream it uses it as a bound, a role a roofline fills when no upstream exists. This is the evidence for H5 that we have: necessary, since a bank that did not transfer across two architectures would not transfer further, but not sufficient, since both campaigns were attention and the 72 bank entries mined from public sources (§2.4) have not yet steered an agent. The experiment that would test both, and whether the bank can replace the human at decision points, is described in §6.

6 Discussion

Did a human expert do the work?

The human wrote no kernel code, and the messages name measurements, layers, and process rather than mechanisms: of the 63 interrogative ones, 17 mention an attention concept and none prescribes a CUDA construct (§5.6). The human did have systems expertise and used it to decide which measurement to demand and when; we claim only that the questions, once asked, are short, generic, and now written down. The agent wrote all 13.8K lines of the two kernels. Whether the bank can replace the human is the experiment this paper does not contain. Its design is fixed: start from the released Blackwell kernel on one of its remaining gaps (dense long context or head dimension 96), hold the model and budget constant, and compare four arms: the equipped loop, the bare agent with the harness alone, the bare agent with a questioner that draws from the bank at plateaus and claimed limits, and a human questioner.

Does KernelSeek need a reference implementation?

The method does not: the harness checks correctness against the seed and an fp32 reference, the goal is a predicate over the seed, and the bank phrases every bound as a roofline or a cycle budget. The case study had one, and used it in two roles. As a yardstick it set the goal and scored the result. As a bound it let a question overturn a claimed ceiling, and this role is the one that mattered; it is filled without a reference by a roofline, a speed-of-light estimate Lin and others (2026), a launcher-only A/B, or a kernel for a neighboring shape, each of which the bank asks for by name. A reference buys a cheaper and sharper bound, and no more: the equipped agent had far more of it in its prompt and gained nothing. The no-reference campaign, where the seed is the fastest kernel known, is the setting the released agent targets and the one we have not yet run.

Threats to validity.

The head-to-head is a single run per arm, with different front-ends and a steered arm against an unsteered one; we control the task, evaluator, hardware, baseline, and correctness gate, and count the human turns in the steered arm’s budget. The case study is one operator family where a strong upstream existed. Wall-clock speedups include dispatch overhead, which inflates the edge sets (Appendix B). The kernels were built before the traces were analyzed, and one author labeled the messages, so the taxonomy may fit the sessions we had; every trace is released so the labeling can be checked.

Limitations and future work.

The Hopper kernel loses on fp8 dense prefill and softcapped prefill, and the Blackwell kernel does not yet build fp8 inputs or dense head dimensions of 192 and above; neither covers the backward pass. The next targets are other deep kernels (latent-attention decode, grouped GEMMs for mixture-of-experts layers, fused collectives, persistent megakernels Jin et al. (2026)) and end-to-end evaluation on the production path Oliaro et al. (2026).

7 Related Work

LLM agents for GPU kernels.

Benchmarks score single operators Ouyang et al. (2025); Zhang et al. (2026), serving kernels on Blackwell Xing et al. (2026); Cao et al. (2026), production shapes against a speed-of-light bound Lin and others (2026), and, in FastKernels Oliaro et al. (2026), agent-written kernels inside the production modules they replace, where kernel-level speedups of several times shrink to at most 1.25×\times end to end. The systems divide along the structure–freedom axis of §1. Scripted agents train a policy inside a fixed loop Baronio et al. (2026); Li et al. (2026); Liu et al. (2026); Zhu et al. (2026); Dai et al. (2026), search over a menu of optimizations Hong et al. (2025); Gai et al. (2026), or assign fixed roles to several agents Wei et al. (2025); Sun et al. (2026b); MIT HAN Lab (2026); Luo et al. (2026); Sun et al. (2026a). Open-ended agents make an LLM the mutation operator of an evolutionary search Romera-Paredes et al. (2024); Novikov et al. (2025); Lange et al. (2025a); Guo et al. (2025); Wiedemann et al. (2026); Yuksekgonul et al. (2026); Lange et al. (2025b); Varadharajan et al. (2026) or, in AVO Chen et al. (2026), a self-directed coding agent; Meta Liao and others (2025) and Cursor with NVIDIA Cursor and NVIDIA (2026) run such loops across whole kernel libraries. AVO is the closest work in target. The closest in spirit is the harness-engineering report of Shui et al. Shui et al. (2026), which finds that agent-assisted optimization beats fully autonomous agents on every FlashInfer contest kernel but does not isolate what the human contributes. No prior work compares two steering strategies on the same target, evaluator, and hardware.

LLMs as optimizers.

The failure modes we attribute to autonomous agents are each documented in isolation: greedy, prior-driven search Redko et al. (2026); Dong et al. (2025); Li et al. (2025), anchoring on the solution in the prompt Jones and Steinhardt (2022), failure to explore without intervention Krishnamurthy et al. (2024), conservatism and premature stopping Merouani et al. (2025), early lock-in under iterative refinement Javaji et al. (2025), and false completion claims Advani (2026). We show them co-occurring in one well-equipped agent.

Questions and self-correction.

Self-Ask Press et al. (2023), Self-Refine Madaan et al. (2023), and Reflexion Shinn et al. (2023) have the model question itself, but intrinsic self-correction is limited Huang et al. (2024) and models defer to the framing they are given Sharma et al. (2024). External feedback works where self-feedback does not: human feedback on a model’s own code raises repair success by more than half, partly because humans propose the structural changes the model does not Olausson et al. (2024), and stating hypotheses before writing programs improves program synthesis Wang et al. (2024). These works use questions to improve one answer; we use them to decide what to measure next in a long-horizon search, in the tradition of Pólya’s heuristics Pólya (1945).

Scaffolding, compilers, and kernels.

An agent’s interface moves its performance Yang et al. (2024), simpler pipelines often win Xia et al. (2024); Schluntz and Zhang (2024), and more tools and context have costs LangChain (2025); Liu et al. (2024); KernelSeek is a data point for the second camp with a twist, since it used more tools than the equipped agent, but on demand. Korch Hu et al. (2024) and Event Tensor Jin et al. (2026) automate a different layer, how kernels are grouped and scheduled into persistent megakernels, and are complementary targets for an agent that writes kernel bodies. The kernels we compare against are FlashAttention and its successors Dao et al. (2022); Dao (2024); Shah et al. (2024); Zadouri and others (2026), co-designed with CUTLASS Thakkar et al. (2023); FlashInfer Ye et al. (2025); cuDNN NVIDIA (2025); and ThunderKittens Spector et al. (2025), on the operator surface vLLM defines Kwon et al. (2023). To our knowledge ours are the first dependency-free FA3- and FA4-class kernels to match or exceed upstream across that surface.

8 Conclusion

For deep kernel optimization the scarce resource is not information but direction. An autonomous agent equipped with a parsed profiler, retrieval, reference material, and a knowledge store plateaued at half the speed of FlashAttention-3 after 133 steps on a 26-configuration task; the same class of model, given a minimal harness and forty messages of which seventeen were questions, passed it in the same week on the same machine. The questions that mattered contained no answers: they moved the agent to a layer it had not examined or made it defend a limit it had declared. KernelSeek packages this: an operator-agnostic agent that makes a CUDA seed faster with no faster implementation to imitate, a verifiable goal enforced by the harness, a question bank the agent applies to itself, and an evolutionary wrapper whose directives are questions. Its case-study output, dependency-free FlashAttention kernels for Hopper and Blackwell, correct on every scenario and faster than upstream, is released with the harness, the bank, and every trace.

AI Usage Disclosure

AI coding agents are the subject of this paper, and they produced most of its artifacts. The two kernels, fa3_hopper.cu and fa4_blackwell.cu, were written entirely by the agents described in §2 (Claude Opus models, claude-opus-4-8 and claude-opus-5, run through Claude Code and Cursor) under human steering; no author wrote or edited kernel code. The baseline agent of §3 was itself built by Claude Code from a written specification, and its runs used claude-opus-4-8. The evaluator, the search scripts, and the PTX probes were written by the same agents under the same steering. The complete traces of every session are released.

The trace analysis of §5 used AI assistance to parse the session logs, classify tool calls by target, and aggregate counts; the human-message labels were assigned by an author. The figures were produced by scripts written with AI assistance from the released data. All reported numbers were re-derived by the authors from the released artifacts.

The question bank of Appendix A was drafted with AI assistance from the traces and from the public sources it cites, and edited by the authors. The manuscript was drafted and revised with AI writing assistance under the authors’ direction; the authors specified the argument, structure, and claims, reviewed and rewrote the text, verified every number against the artifacts, and take responsibility for all content.

Appendix A The Full Question Bank

The bank has three layers. The first is the released bank of 101 core questions plus an operator plug-in (§2.3), organized by where a performance gap might be and meant to be worked through in order, so that the scope, the bound, the harness, the host, and the routing are settled before the kernel body is touched. The second is the list of questions the skill asks the agent to put to itself at every iteration. The third is the set of question categories observed in the human messages of the case study, with verbatim examples.

Every core entry satisfies five admission rules. It carries no answer: it names a class of hypothesis or a quantity to measure, never a technique to apply. It is answerable by a measurement with stock tools (the profiler, the disassembler, the assembler’s resource report, clock counters, the harness). It is phrased against a bound, a roofline or a per-tile cycle budget, never against a reference implementation; the five questions that only make sense when another implementation is available to measure form their own conditional group. It names an architecture only as a parameter, and must make sense on Ampere, Hopper, and Blackwell alike. And it names no operator: the attention structure the case study needed (paging, softmax, split-KV, grouped heads) lives in a plug-in that the template at the end of this section describes.

Tags: [G] generic; [A], [H], [B] Ampere-, Hopper-, or Blackwell-specific checklist. Provenance tags give where each question came from: tr, the human messages and skill of our traces; sb, ps, and mo, three public GEMM optimization worklogs on Ampere Boehm (2022), Hopper Shankhdhar (2024), and Blackwell Modular Inc. (2025); fa3 and fa4, the FlashAttention-3 and -4 papers Shah et al. (2024); Zadouri and others (2026). The first bank, distilled from the traces alone after the campaigns, had 48 entries of which 21 named the upstream kernel as the comparison and 13 named attention structure; the released bank is the result of removing both, which moved 11 entries into the plug-in, rewrote 27, kept 10, and added the rest from the public sources. The 72 entries whose provenance is the public sources alone have not yet been exercised by our agent.

A.1 Core Bank

A. Scope and triage.

  1. 1.

    Which losing scenarios share a kernel body, and which only share a host launcher? [G, tr]

  2. 2.

    Do the losers form one regime (large, small, irregular extents, padded dimension) or a grab bag? [G, tr]

  3. 3.

    Which problem dimension does the gap grow with: the streamed one (feed), the tiled one (tiling, scheduling), or none (a fixed tax)? [G, tr]

  4. 4.

    Is the gap in kernel cycles at locked clocks, or only in wall-clock (host, just-in-time compile, launch)? [G, tr]

  5. 5.

    Of the gaps and fixes I am listing, which have I already tried in this campaign, and why did they fail? [G, tr]

  6. 6.

    What do the scenarios below the target have in common, grouped by cause rather than by shape? [G, tr]

B. Bound and regime.

  1. 7.

    From the minimum bytes and FLOPs for this shape, which bound should dominate, and does the measured time match it? [G, sb]

  2. 8.

    Am I memory-, compute-, latency-, or launch-bound on this scenario, and does the answer change across the suite? [G, sb, ps]

  3. 9.

    For my tile, what are the cycle counts per unit (MMA, special-function, FMA, shared memory, L2 and DRAM), and which is largest? [G, fa4]

  4. 10.

    What is this GPU’s ratio of MMA to special-function throughput, and does my instruction mix exceed it? [G, fa3, fa4]

  5. 11.

    Is the peak I measure against the right one: locked clocks, the power state the benchmark runs at, this data type’s MMA rate? [G, ps]

  6. 12.

    Does shared-memory traffic scale with the number of MMA instructions rather than with tile size, and is it the binder? [G, fa4]

  7. 13.

    Could a power or thermal limit, not the kernel, be the ceiling at this size? [G, ps]

C. Harness and measurement.

  1. 14.

    Is the win larger than the noise measured now on this GPU, not the noise of an earlier run? [G, tr]

  2. 15.

    Am I timing what I think I am timing: warm-ups, cache flush, the same input distribution and data type as the baseline, kernel-only versus end-to-end? [G, sb, ps]

  3. 16.

    Is any of my time outside the kernel: metadata builds, combine passes, device-to-host copies, counter resets, descriptor builds? [G, tr]

  4. 17.

    Does the result hold on production-shaped problems, not only on the square or power-of-two sizes I tuned on? [G, mo, ps]

  5. 18.

    Have I recorded clocks, power state, warm-up count, iteration count, and variance before claiming a fraction of peak? [G, mo]

D. Host, launch, routing.

  1. 19.

    Is there a synchronous device-to-host copy left on the losing route that another route already avoids? [G, tr]

  2. 20.

    Is work redone per call on the host (descriptors, gather maps, schedules) that could be built once and cached? [G, tr, fa4]

  3. 21.

    Are there clears of counters, partial buffers, or outputs that nothing reads, or that could be fused? [G, tr]

  4. 22.

    For small grids, is the gap launch and setup overhead, with kernel-only time already near the bound? [G, tr]

  5. 23.

    Is this shape on the kernel I think it is, or on an older path because a routing gate is stale? [G, tr]

  6. 24.

    Would forcing the intended kernel on this shape, where numerically safe, close the gap without touching the kernel? [G, tr]

  7. 25.

    Is a feature flag or shape parameter forcing a slow instantiation that deserves its own specialization? [G, tr, sb]

  8. 26.

    For single-tile or underfilled grids, would a smaller tile or a split along the reduction dimension fill the machine? [G, tr, sb]

E. Memory hierarchy and data movement.

  1. 27.

    What is the achieved global-memory throughput against peak, and does the profiler flag uncoalesced or sector-inefficient accesses? [G, sb]

  2. 28.

    Does the SASS show the widest loads and stores for every operand, or are some still 32-bit? [G, sb]

  3. 29.

    Where the compiler refuses to vectorize, can I prove alignment to it instead of unrolling by hand? [G, sb]

  4. 30.

    Are shared-memory bank conflicts reported for the exact access pattern the MMA reads, and does fixing them help end to end? [G, sb, mo]

  5. 31.

    What is the L2 hit rate, and which concurrently resident CTAs actually share input data? [G, sb, ps]

  6. 32.

    Do neighboring CTAs load identical tiles that one load could serve? [G, ps, mo]

  7. 33.

    Are outputs written coalesced and vectorized through shared memory, with streaming hints where they are never re-read? [G, mo, ps]

  8. 34.

    Would a contiguous version of the same math meet the bound? If so, the gap is in the indirect or gathered loads. [G, tr]

  9. 35.

    Do intermediates round-trip through shared or on-chip memory more than once between producers and consumers? [G, tr]

  10. 36.

    Before tuning the epilogue, have I confirmed that the main loop is no longer bandwidth-bound? [G, mo]

F. Compute issue and instruction mix.

  1. 37.

    What dominates the instruction mix, math or address arithmetic and loads, and what is the FLOPs-per-load ratio per thread? [G, sb]

  2. 38.

    Am I using the widest MMA shape the instruction set offers, and what does the wider one cost in registers and shared memory? [G, ps, fa4]

  3. 39.

    Does the compiler already do the caching, unrolling, or reordering I am about to hand-write? [G, sb]

  4. 40.

    Is the non-MMA work (exponentials, conversions, reductions, rescaling) executing concurrently with the MMAs, or serialized by waits? [G, fa3, fa4]

  5. 41.

    Did I confirm the intended overlap in the SASS or a timeline, rather than assuming source order survived the compiler? [G, fa3]

  6. 42.

    Can part of a bottlenecked unit’s work be re-expressed on an idle unit, and what fraction balances them? [G, fa4]

  7. 43.

    Which per-iteration bookkeeping is only occasionally necessary, and can it be made conditional while staying warp-uniform? [G, fa4]

  8. 44.

    Am I doing per-element work (masking, bounds checks, predication) on tiles that are provably full or provably empty? [G, tr]

  9. 45.

    Do concurrent warps contend for the same slow unit at the same time, and should their critical sections be staggered? [G, fa3]

  10. 46.

    Are there type conversions or silent up-casts on the hot path? [G, tr]

G. Occupancy, registers, shared memory.

  1. 47.

    From registers, shared memory, and threads per block, what occupancy is achievable, and do the stall reasons say more would help? [G, sb]

  2. 48.

    Is the binding limit the per-thread register cap rather than the register file, suggesting splitting the work across more warps? [G, ps]

  3. 49.

    Does the assembler warn about serialized MMAs or spills, and do I see local-memory traffic in the SASS? [G, ps]

  4. 50.

    Per warp role, what is the register budget for inputs, outputs, and temporaries, and does the sum fit? [G, fa4]

  5. 51.

    Are registers reallocated from issue-only warps to compute warps, and is the split tuned? [G, fa3, ps]

  6. 52.

    Can partial results be stored or consumed early to shorten live ranges? [G, fa4]

  7. 53.

    Did I size the multistage buffer from the shared-memory budget or pick a stage count, and do stages and output buffers compete? [G, mo]

  8. 54.

    For dimensions that are not multiples of the MMA tile, am I on padded math, and is a native-width instantiation possible? [G, tr]

  9. 55.

    Does my thread-to-data mapping need cross-lane shuffles for reductions, or could another mapping remove them? [G, fa4]

H. Asynchrony and pipelining.

  1. 56.

    Measured in cycles, how long are the load, compute, and store phases per tile, and which is not overlapped? [G, ps]

  2. 57.

    Have I drawn the dependency chain of one iteration and found which link leaves a unit idle? [G, mo]

  3. 58.

    Are data movement, MMA issue, and the non-MMA math in separate warps, or does one warp do all three in sequence? [G, fa3, mo]

  4. 59.

    How many independent MMAs are in flight, and is that enough to cover the non-MMA latency on this architecture? [G, fa4]

  5. 60.

    Are asynchronous operations committed without immediate waits, with the wait placed just before the consumer? [G, fa3]

  6. 61.

    Is the multistage pipeline at full depth on the losers, or draining early on partial tiles? [G, tr]

  7. 62.

    Which true dependence serializes the inner loop, and would one extra buffer let iteration j+1j{+}1 overlap iteration jj? [G, fa3]

  8. 63.

    Is the store path overlapped with the next tile’s compute, or a serial tail? [G, mo, ps]

  9. 64.

    How many synchronizations per tile does the barrier API cost, and is the primitive itself the overhead? [G, ps]

  10. 65.

    Is any asynchronous wait or barrier issued under a divergent predicate? [G, tr]

  11. 66.

    For a deeper pipeline I adopted or rejected, did I weigh its register cost against the forced tile-size reduction? [G, fa3]

I. Scheduling and load balance.

  1. 67.

    Does the tile count divide evenly into the SM count on the shapes that matter, or is there a tail wave? [G, mo, ps]

  2. 68.

    In what order are tiles assigned to SMs, and would grouping or a space-filling curve raise L2 reuse? [G, ps, mo]

  3. 69.

    Would a persistent kernel help, and does its tile order preserve the locality the hardware scheduler gave me? [G, ps]

  4. 70.

    Does the kernel pay launch, shared-memory, and barrier re-initialization per tile instead of per CTA lifetime? [G, mo]

  5. 71.

    Where variable extents or masks make tiles unequal, which tiles are the long tail, and are they issued first? [G, fa4]

  6. 72.

    For data-dependent work sizes, is the schedule computed once and cached? [G, fa4]

  7. 73.

    If work is split along the reduction dimension, is the split heuristic, the combine, or the partial-buffer traffic the cost? [G, tr]

  8. 74.

    Do contended global reductions run on dedicated warps, in an order that avoids stall chains? [G, fa3, fa4]

J. Low-precision numerics.

  1. 75.

    What operand layout does the low-precision MMA require, and where is the fix-up done and hidden? [G, fa3]

  2. 76.

    Is the quantization-scale granularity matched to my tile, so that scaling rides on existing multiplies? [G, fa3]

  3. 77.

    What precision does the downstream consumer need, and did I measure error after that rounding against a high-precision reference? [G, fa4]

  4. 78.

    For any approximation or skipped step, is there a final exact normalization that bounds the drift? [G, fa4]

K. If another implementation of this operator is available to measure.

  1. 79.

    Am I comparing against its steady-state binary, not a cold just-in-time compile or a first-call path? [G, tr]

  2. 80.

    Same buffers, data type, flags, and split count as its call? [G, tr]

  3. 81.

    Which of its kernels is dispatched for this shape, and does it use a trick (a split, a specialization) that I do not? [G, sb]

  4. 82.

    On the same scenario, how do its measured unit utilizations and stall reasons differ from mine, and which difference matches my gap? [G, tr]

  5. 83.

    Is it constrained by the same rules as I am? If so and it is faster, which of my claimed limits does its existence refute? [G, tr]

L. Ampere-class checklist.

  1. 84.

    Am I on tensor-core MMA with matrix-fragment loads from shared memory, or on scalar FMA? [A, sb, ps]

  2. 85.

    Is global-to-shared staging asynchronous and double-buffered at both the global-to-shared and shared-to-register levels? [A, sb]

  3. 86.

    Are block, warp, and thread tiles chosen by autotuning on this GPU, with the grid filtered for alignment constraints? [A, sb]

  4. 87.

    Did the bank-conflict fix pay for itself, or did the layout change cost more than the conflicts? [A, sb]

M. Hopper checklist.

  1. 88.

    Are the MMAs the asynchronous warpgroup kind, with accumulators in registers budgeted per warpgroup? [H, ps, fa3]

  2. 89.

    Are tile loads done by the dedicated copy engine with a swizzle that matches the MMA’s shared-memory layout? [H, ps]

  3. 90.

    Do producer warps release registers to consumers, with the split tuned to the accumulator footprint? [H, ps, fa3]

  4. 91.

    Are neighboring CTAs in a cluster multicasting shared operands, and was the cluster size tuned? [H, ps]

  5. 92.

    Are the barriers raw memory barriers with manual phase tracking, or a higher-level API that adds synchronizations? [H, ps]

  6. 93.

    Is the epilogue staged through shared memory and stored asynchronously, and does that trade against pipeline depth? [H, ps]

N. Blackwell checklist.

  1. 94.

    Are the MMAs fully asynchronous into tensor memory, issued by one thread, with completion signaled through barriers rather than waits? [B, mo, fa4]

  2. 95.

    Is tensor memory allocated once per CTA lifetime, and could its columns be split so the next tile accumulates while the last drains? [B, mo]

  3. 96.

    Is the accumulator layout in tensor memory spilling or serializing the MMA against the consumer warps? [B, tr]

  4. 97.

    Would a two-SM MMA pair halve per-SM operand traffic and shared-memory footprint for this tile? [B, mo, fa4]

  5. 98.

    Is only the leader CTA issuing MMAs, with peer barriers arrived at cluster scope? [B, mo]

  6. 99.

    Is a static tile scheduler assuming all SMs are free where the hardware launch-control scheduler could rebalance, and is scheduler latency hidden under the next load? [B, mo]

  7. 100.

    Is tensor-memory-to-register traffic off the critical path, and which register-resident fix-ups can move to a separate warp? [B, fa4]

  8. 101.

    Given that the special-function unit did not scale with the MMA on this architecture, what fraction of that unit’s work must move elsewhere? [B, fa4]

O. Operator plug-in template.

A plug-in supplies, for one operator, five things: its regimes; its irregular-work structure; its non-MMA units; its reduction splits; and its indirect loads. Each has a generic ancestor in the core (entries 2, 71, 40, 73, and 34 respectively), so the core already asks about it in the abstract and the plug-in only names the instance. The attention plug-in used in the case study lists, as regimes, prefill versus decode, dense versus paged key–value cache, short versus long context, and grouped or multi-query heads; as irregular work, causal and sliding-window masks and variable lengths; as non-MMA units, the softmax exponential and the online rescale; as reduction split, split-KV decode and its combine; and as indirect loads, page-table gathers. Its eleven questions (whether grouped and multi-query losers show the same relative gap as multi-head at equal tokens; whether the softmax and correction of two stacked tile halves overlap or serialize; whether a paged loser is still feed-latency-bound after the gather and preload fixes; whether contiguous loads on the same math would meet the bound; whether the hardware gather or a coalesced asynchronous copy is the right loader; whether short decodes pay gather and descriptor setup that does not amortize; whether the gap tracks page fragmentation; whether the decoupled key and value rings are balanced on the unequal-head-dimension path; whether softmax, rescale, and masking between MMAs burn issue slots that specialized warps would hide; whether the split-KV heuristic, the combine, or the partial buffers are the cost; and whether paged-to-contiguous on the same problem size closes the gap) are the attention instances of core entries 2, 45, 34, 34, 34, 22, 34, 61, 40, 73, and 34.

A.2 The Skill’s “Ask Yourself” List

The skill (§2.5) instructs the agent to ask itself the following at every iteration:

  1. 1.

    Which bound binds on this scenario (bandwidth, MMA, special-function unit, shared-memory bandwidth, issue slots, launch), and what fraction of it do we reach?

  2. 2.

    Is the gap in kernel cycles, or outside the kernel (host, launch, routing, harness)?

  3. 3.

    Which single unit or stage has the largest excess over its cycle budget, and what is my hypothesis for why?

  4. 4.

    Do the losing scenarios share one cause, and have I grouped them before fixing any?

  5. 5.

    Should the losing regime have its own kernel instead of a flag in a shared one?

  6. 6.

    Is every asynchronous mechanism this architecture offers actually asynchronous in my SASS, or are waits placed where they serialize?

  7. 7.

    Is the win I just measured larger than the noise of this GPU at this moment, and does it hold on the other regimes?

  8. 8.

    If another implementation of this operator can be measured on this machine, how do its profile and launch path differ from mine, and which difference explains my gap?

A.3 Categories Observed in the Human Messages

Table 4 lists the eight categories of §2.3 with verbatim examples from the traces and the outcome they led to where one is documented (§5.4). Counts are over the 162 human messages; a message is counted in a category when its primary act was a question or a question-shaped correction of that kind. Eight further questions concerned repository housekeeping and are omitted.

Appendix B Case-Study Kernel Details

B.1 fa3_hopper.cu

The Hopper kernel is organized as a dispatcher over specialized paths, with the scalar seed retained as the fallback for anything not yet specialized. The fast paths are warp-specialized: one producer warpgroup issues TMA bulk-tensor loads of K and V into a three-stage shared-memory ring ordered by mbarrier phases, while two consumer warpgroups run asynchronous wgmma MMAs on a 128×128128\times 128 CTA tile, with setmaxnreg moving registers from the producer (40 per thread) to the consumers (up to 168). Prefill is persistent: Q tiles arrive by TMA, a dynamic scheduler hands out tiles, and the two consumer warpgroups ping-pong so that one warpgroup’s softmax overlaps the other’s MMAs. Masking is resolved per tile into a [l​o,h​i)[lo,hi) key range so that fully visible tiles skip the mask and fully masked tiles exit before the main loop. Decode uses a separate kernel with split-KV and a combine pass, with split heuristics chosen per shape. The fp8 path runs native e4m3 wgmma; for head dimension 64 it pads the Q and K tiles to 128 columns so that the 128-byte swizzle stride composes and contracts only over the real columns, which replaced an LSU-bound convert pass and took that scenario from 0.30×\times to 0.98×\times. Attention sinks are folded into the softmax denominator at the epilogue, cache_leftpad is an absolute lower bound on the key index with leading-tile pruning, and unequal head dimensions (192/128) are handled by templating the two dimensions separately in prefill and decode.

The head-dimension-256 limit.

The output accumulator alone takes 128 registers per consumer thread, which forces one CTA per SM and leaves the consumer starved on K/V arrival (NCU: barrier and long-scoreboard bound, tensor pipe at 44%). The hand-written 128-byte swizzle composes only at key-tile widths of 48, 64, and 128; FA3 reaches its width of 80 because CUTLASS’s register allocator schedules that tile without serializing wgmma. A half-height Q tile with a deeper ring (0.72×\times: occupancy, not ring depth, is binding), a 240-register rebalance (deadlocks at the 65,536-register edge), and a head-dimension split (pays a 1.5×\times redundant QK cost) were each measured and lost; the collective rewrite that followed brought the scenario to 0.94×\times in the final measurement.

Per-set results.

The Hopper suite is the same 182 scenario definitions as Blackwell’s, all of which fa3_hopper.cu supports. Over the FA3 test grids (attntest, 64): 1.22×\times, 54 at or above parity, worst 0.89. Over the masking and boundary grid (edge, 31): 1.55×\times, 30 at or above parity. Over the paper-style sweeps (claim, 77): 1.01×\times, 44 at or above parity, with the per-group geomeans ranging from 0.67 (dense fp8 prefill, 8 scenarios) through 0.87 (causal d=256d=256), 0.92 (causal d=128d=128), 0.96 (prefill) and 1.05 (chunked prefill) to 1.20 (decode up to 4K), 1.22 (speculative decode) and 1.38 (ragged prefill). Over the production shapes (real, 10): 1.10×\times, 7 at or above parity. cuDNN 9.20 fused SDPA, fed the same packed and paged buffers, supports 145 of the 182 and runs at 0.86×\times FA3 in geomean; fa3_hopper.cu is faster on 111 of them, with cuDNN winning dense prefill by up to 1.6×\times and losing paged decode by up to 5.5×\times. FlashInfer supports 32 and runs at 0.72×\times FA3; fa3_hopper.cu is faster on all 32. The worst Hopper scenarios are dense fp8 prefill at d=64d=64 and 8K context (0.34×\times), a softcapped 4K prefill (0.51×\times), d=96d=96 (0.71×\times), and a 4K sliding window (0.79×\times). Table 5 lists every scenario.

B.2 fa4_blackwell.cu

The Blackwell kernel is a family with configuration-aware routing on the host:

  • •

    fwd_kernel_fa4: a persistent warp-specialized collective with a 256-row Q tile as two stacked 128-row halves sharing K and V, two softmax warpgroups in an ordered ping-pong, a correction warpgroup rescaling O in tensor memory with packed f32x2 math, one MMA warp, and load warps, in a 512-thread CTA with a 192/64/64 register plan, longest-processing-time persistent scheduling, and continuous cross-tile overlap. Sliding windows, attention sinks, padded head dimension 96, and paged KV are if constexpr template parameters; the default instantiation is SASS-byte-identical to the ungrafted kernel.

  • •

    fwd_kernel_fa4dk: the same for dq​k=192,dv=128d_{qk}=192,d_{v}=128 with a decoupled K-depth-2, V-depth-1 ring that fits the 227 KB shared-memory cap (0.21×\times to 1.06×\times).

  • •

    fwd_kernel_fa4_paged: the same choreography on a paged gather. Pages aligned to the 8-row swizzle atom load as TMA boxes (8 per tile instead of about 4,096 cp.async issues); other page sizes use a warp-uniform tile::gather4 loader (the divergent-lane version had made TMA issue 29.5% of all executed instructions); a run detector upgrades tiles whose physical pages are consecutive to full-width boxes at run time.

  • •

    fwd_kernel_ws2 and the paged decode kernels for small, ragged, and decode shapes, with split-KV and a combine pass.

Host-side design: no route performs a synchronous device-to-host copy (one cu_seqlens.to(cpu) cost about 38 μ\mus per call and had hidden a kernel already faster than upstream); the persistent scheduler’s counter resets itself on device; large-query paged prefill with page sizes the TMA box cannot express is materialized once into a contiguous cache (two passes over the unique bytes, under 1% of the attention’s own traffic) and routed to the dense kernel; and mixed batches are split by query length into two launches so that decode sequences read K/V once per KV head.

Remaining known costs

, in order of measured size: a K/V ring of two pairs where the shared-memory budget would admit two and a half; all ex2 on the XU pipe, with no fraction emulated on the FMA pipe; the correction warpgroup also running the epilogue rather than a separate warp; page rows staged through shared memory rather than held in registers; and a software row-max instead of the hardware reduction.

Scenario sets.

attntest (64): the FA3 grids ported to FA4. edge (31): a dense (sq,sk)(s_{q},s_{k}) masking and boundary grid from FA4’s own tests. claim (77): causal and non-causal sweeps over sequence length and head dimension in the style of the FA4 paper, plus decode, chunked prefill, speculative, mixed-batch, and fp8-KV groups. real (10): GQA shapes from SOL-ExecBench (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen3-30B-A3B; decode and paged prefill; page size 1).

Caveats.

The Blackwell edge kernels take 50–100 μ\mus under FA4, so its 2.0×\times is dominated by FA4’s Python and CuteDSL dispatch; kernel-only ratios there are near parity. The Hopper edge set (1.55×\times) is in the same short-kernel regime against FA3’s compiled op and its scheduler-metadata call, and should be read with the same caution. The six bf16-query/fp8-KV decode scenarios in claim run at 4.5–9.9×\times because FA4 is slow on them; excluding them gives 1.37×\times vs. upstream, 1.32×\times vs. fastest open-source, and 1.08×\times vs. fastest available over the remaining 118. The run-detecting TMA path benefits from the harness building page tables with arange; with it disabled, the two long-context decode scenarios fall from 1.01 and 0.90 to 0.77 and 0.78×\times. Noise is about ±\pm1.5% for repeated single-GPU runs and ±\pm5% across four-GPU sweeps.

Where it loses, with causes.

Dense long context (0.88–0.92×\times) executes exactly FA4’s tensor work (identical tcgen05 op counts per block) over 33% more cycles; the idle tensor pipe is attributable to twice as many mbarrier waits per block (47.7 vs. 24.5), with memory, occupancy, and the softmax transcendentals measured and ruled out. Batch-64 decode (0.88×\times) pays a cold start per CTA over 3.5 waves where FA4 runs a persistent grid. Head dimension 96 (0.85×\times) runs on the padded 128-wide path. A mixed prefill/decode batch (0.78×\times) is within its historical noise band. Production shapes: short-context decode 1.50 and 1.49×\times FA4 (Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen3-30B at 512 tokens), long-context decode 1.17 and 1.01×\times (4K and 16K), paged prefill 1.04, 0.98, and 0.91×\times.
