Appendix D Trace Statistics and Methodology

Sources.

Sixteen KernelSeek sessions are archived: nine Claude Code sessions as JSONL transcripts with their subagent transcripts, and seven Cursor sessions as exported JSONL. Claude Code transcripts record the model per assistant message (claude-opus-4-8 in seven sessions, claude-opus-5 in two); Cursor exports do not. The equipped agent’s run is a checkpoint directory with one record per candidate (source, build, correctness, timing, promotion decision, timestamp) and the orchestrator’s log, memory file, and knowledge store.

Parsing.

A tool call is an assistant content block of type tool use, de-duplicated by its identifier across the parent transcript and any compaction summaries; a subagent’s calls are counted separately and attributed to the parent session. Human turns are user messages that are not tool results, Stop-hook injections, or system reminders; in Cursor exports they are identified by the user record’s timestamp tag. Tool calls are classified by regular expressions over the tool name and arguments into: profiler runs, SASS or PTX inspections, builds, benchmark or evaluator runs, documentation reads, sanitizer runs, and reads of the agent’s own kernel files; the categories overlap where a shell command does two things. The “tool-result text re-reading own kernel” figure of Table 2 is the share of tool-result characters returned by file reads whose path is one of the kernel sources, over all tool-result characters in the Claude Code parent transcripts (26%; for the equipped agent, the same quantity over its per-step tool logs, 82%).

Labeling.

One author labeled each of the 162 human messages by its primary act (goal, directive, question, approval, correction), flagged whether it was phrased as a question, and assigned the 44 question-act messages and the 12 question-shaped corrections to the categories of §2.3; eight further questions concerned repository housekeeping and are excluded from Figure 4(b). The agent-side counts (35 structured questions to the human, 24 offering to accept or stop, 126 limit assertions, 59 Stop-hook returns) are from the Claude Code sessions only, where these events are structured; the Cursor exports do not separate them. Figure 4 shows the resulting distribution. The labels, the parsing scripts, and the per-session inventory are released with the traces.

Appendix E Baseline Agent Details

Table 7 lists the components of Arsenal and what each contributed to the step prompt. The per-step prompt assembled, in order: the task statement and hard rules; the chosen lever with its rationale; the NCU diagnosis for the worst configuration; the SASS instruction-mix deltas against the champion; the retrieved documentation sections; the reference-library hints; the knowledge-store notes matching the lever; the memory file’s recent lessons; the current champion source; and the instruction to write one improved candidate to a fixed path and stop. The median prompt was 22.6K characters excluding the champion source, 37% of it retrieved or pre-fetched material. Promotion required a correct candidate whose worst-configuration ratio exceeded the champion’s by more than a 3% noise band. The plateau detector fired after eight steps without promotion and opened a rewrite branch seeded at the lineage’s pre-plateau knee; 37 branches were opened, 36 from the same step. Three human rollbacks discarded 117 steps. The run’s 313 kept steps, the 133 model-driven ones among them, the memory file, and the knowledge store are released with the specification from which the agent was built.

Appendix F Benchmark Methodology

Timing.

Each scenario is timed on one GPU with every implementation run back to back from byte-identical inputs. After 20 warm-up calls, the harness takes three trials of 40 CUDA-event samples each, flushing a 32 MB buffer through L2 and synchronizing before every sample, and reports the median of the 120 samples; the per-scenario speedup is the upstream median over the implementation’s median. Clocks are not locked, which is why only ratios are reported. cuDNN and FlashInfer are given the same packed and paged buffers as our kernel and the upstream, and a scenario is marked unsupported for an implementation when it rejects the configuration or fails correctness.

Correctness.

Every candidate’s outputs are compared with the upstream kernel’s and with an fp32 reference on every scenario, with a per-dtype tolerance; a candidate that fails any scenario scores zero. In the head-to-head, the equipped agent’s gate additionally required token-for-token equality with FA3 on a greedy decode inside vLLM.

Repeats and noise.

The Hopper suite was run as three full repeats in each of four independent batches on the 8×\timesH200 node, one scenario per GPU at a time, with a single-GPU serial control that agrees with the parallel runs to within 0.8%. Per-scenario medians over the three repeats are the reported numbers; the four batches agree to within 0.3% on every aggregate, and per-scenario ratios vary by 1% at the median and 6% at most. The Blackwell suite was run once on the 8×\timesB200 node with the same protocol. The edge scenarios are short kernels for which dispatch overhead is a visible share of wall-clock time, so their ratios overstate kernel-only gains; the claim and real sets are long enough that dispatch is negligible.
